column1: Notes:
We use emission intensities by pollutant by fuel from EPA or the GREET1 model, which
provide different intensities depending on which technology is burning a given
fuel.
For the US, we manually set all CO2 emissions factors for transportation biofuels to 0 to align with EPA
Inventory reporting. However, we leave in guidance about using this file for transportation biofuels for other countries.
Tailpipe vs. Lifecycle
For the most part, the emissions indices in this file are tailpipe emissions indices.
However, only for the pollutant CO2, and only for biofuel gasoline, biofuel diesel,
and biomass, we subtract the CO2 that was sequestered in the course of creating
these fuels, resulting in a lifecycle emissions index rather than a tailpipe emissions
index.  This must be done for the two liquid biofuels in order for elements of the
Transportation sector to work correctly- particularly the Low Carbon Fuel Standard policy.
We apply the same treatment to biomass for consistency.
Note that this assumes that CO2 sequestration from producing the biofuels or
biomass in the BAU case is NOT already factored into the Industry or Land Use
sectors' input data.  If this assumption is violated, then CO2 sequestration from
producing the BAU case quantity of biofuels and biomass will be double-counted.
This may not be problematic for some EPS regional adaptations, if there is
little to no biofuel or biomass production in the BAU case.
If you wish to use tailpipe rather than lifecycle CO2 emissions for biofuel
gasoline, biofuel diesel, and biomass, you can toggle the switch below to do
so.  NOTE that the low-carbon fuel standard (both the BAU version and the
policy lever) will not work correctly if you use tailpipe emissions indices.
This may not be a problem if you are adapting the model to a country or
region with no BAU LCFS-like policy and you have no interest in using the
LCFS policy lever when designing policy packages.
TRUE

column1: Biofuel Mappings
GREET includes a number of different biofuels that could be considered "biofuel
gasoline" or "biofuel diesel."
Generic "renewable gasoline" or "biodiesel" emissions indices are available for
some combustion technologies.  We use these, when available.  In other cases (such as
for LDVs and motorbikes), we need to select the
best specific biofuels to represent each of the two biofuel subscripts in the model.
We also need to make this selection to convert CO2 from tailpipe to lifecycle emissions
(as noted above) for all combustion technologies.
We prefer values for these fuels when they are pure, not blends (that is, no blend
such as E15 or BD20), because the transportation sector and the LCFS policy assume
these subscripts refer to the biofuel portion, even if it is ultimately blended before
use.  However, emissions indices are not provided for any pure ethanol fuel in GREET.
Accordingly, we use emissions indices for the most similar fuel, E85.
Thus, mappings for emissions indices purposes are:
biofuel gasoline

Transportation Sector
Note that not all of the vehicle/fuel type combinations reported by GREET1 and included in
this spreadsheet are actually used or usable in the model.  For example, currently no
ships use natural gas as a fuel type, and there is no policy lever that can cause them to do so.
Because EPA's Mobile Combustion tables report CH4 and N2O emissions per mile rather than per
gallon, the CH4 and N2O calculations rely on reported emissions factors for stationary sources.
Non-Transportation Sectors
For non-Transportation sectors, GREET1 disaggregates emissions indices by type of technology
that is combusting the fuel.  We try to use the most representative technology in
GREET1 for each sector in our model.  This is, of course, an approximation.
Although GREET1 has Emissions Indices time series with three points (2010, 2015, 2020)
on the "EF_TS" tab for non-Transportation sectors, we use the non-time series data
from the "EF" tab (which contains 2010 values) for several reasons.
First, this is what GREET1 itself uses by default in its own calculations.
Second, the time series changes on "EF_TS" seem sparse and irregular, with many
emissions indices not changing over time.
Third, this greatly reduces the number of input data tables we need to generate and
read into Vensim, which will help with the portability of the model, particularly
because many countries are unlikely to have future projected time series for
emissions intensities by pollutant by sector by fuel.
In the Electricity sector, for non-CO2, -CH4, and -N2O pollutants, we use values from GREET1's
"Electric" tab, which Argonne NL staff have confirmed are more up-to-date and
better than the values on the "EF" tab for power plants.  (No SOx value is available
for biomass power plants on the "Electric" tab, so we continue to use the value
from the "EF" tab.)
This variable includes output sheets for each industry, but they contain identical
GREET data in the U.S. version.  This is to support other regional EPS adaptations
that may use different emissions intensities for different industries.
Hard Coal and Lignite Split in Power Sector
We use a two part process for customizing some emissions factors for hard coal and lignite in the power sector.
For NOx, and SOx, we use the ratio of weighted emissions factors for different plant types
from eGrid relative to the coal fleet as a whole. We multiply these weighting factors by the emissions
factor from GREEET to develop lignite/hard coal specific factors.
For PM, VOCs, and CO, we use data form EIA Form 923 on heat content and ash content together with
data from EPA's AP-42 emissions factors and eGrid data on boiler types to estimate heat-input and
boiler type weighted emissions factors (uncontrolled) for lignite and hard coal. Because the U.S.
fleet is dominated by bituminous/subbituminous plants (which have the same emissions factors in
AP-42), we multiply the GREET emissions factor for all power sector coal by the lignite:hard coal
emissions factor ratio to develop lignite specific emissions factors.
Petroleum and MSW Plants
These plant types comprise a variety of plants in the US EPS with different characteristics (e.g. for petroleum plants,
plants burning residual fuel oil, petroleum diesel, kerosene, etc.). We therefore take a weighted average emissions factor for all plants
of that type rather than pulling emissions factors based on a single fuel from the EPA source data.
Hydrogen
Hydrogen can either be combusted or used to power a fuel cell.  When combusted,
hydrogen generates high temperatures that break apart some of the N2 molecules in
the air, forming NOx.  When used in a fuel cell, no high temperatures are generated,
so we assume no NOx is formed.
We assume that in non-transportation sectors, hydrogen is predominantly combusted,
and we use GREET emissions factors, which include NOx emissions.
In the Transportation sector, we assume hydrogen is combusted in ships and in rail
locomotives that use hydrogen, and hydrogen is used to power a fuel cell in on-road
vehicles that use hydrogen.
Heating Value Adjustment (only for GREET values)
Fuels have two "heating values" (energy content per unit mass of fuel).  A fuel's "lower" heating
value (also known as the "net calorific value") assumes the latent heat of vaporization of water in
the reaction products is not recovered, while the higher value (the "gross calorific value") takes
into account the latent heat of vaporization of water in the combustion products.  In other words,
the "lower" heating values express the concept that there is less recoverable energy, useful to
do work, per unit mass of fuel.
Fuel use data from the Energy Information Administration is expressed in BTUs of fuel burned
based on the higher heating values of those fuels.  These data are used in many variables
throughout the model.  (Other countries may have different data sources but should
be assumed to be based on gross energy content of fuels, or higher heating values, unless
otherwise specified.)
Therefore, the emissions indices from GREET need to be adjusted to reflect fuels' higher heating
values.  GREET includes the heating values for each fuel on tab "".  There also
is a toggle switch on that tab to tell GREET to use the higher heating values, but that switch only
updates the emissions intensities for certain pollutants (CO2 and SOx) on tab "EF," not all
pollutants.  This is a bug in GREET.  Accordingly, rather than rely on GREET's toggle switch, we
manually adjust the emissions intensities using the ratios of lower and higher heating values
available on that tab.
The adjustment can be disabled by setting the following cell to zero.  Do this only if adapting
the EPS for a non-U.S. country and you are certain that the input data you have for quantity of
fuel used (in energy units) in the various sectors is based on lower heating values.
TRUE

column1: Particulate Emissions Calculations: PMs, VOCs, OC, BC, NOX, SOX for the transportation, buildings, electricity, and industrial sector
We took criteria air pollutant data by sector from the 2017 National Emissions Inventory Data.

We took AEO energy consumption data from 2017 and estimated the criteria air pollutants per energy consumption values. To estimate energy consumption by sector we used the same methods we used to calculate BIFUBC and BCEU.
The 'EPA-data' tab contains data exported directly from the 2017 National Emissions Inventory (NEI) Data Queries. The 'Crosswalk sectors' tab shows how we assigned EPA categories to EPS sectors.

The 'particulates' tab summarizes the EPA data by emissions, sector, and fuel. The 'energy' tab summarizes AEO's 2017 energy consumption data. The 'calcs' tab calculates the pollutant emissions factors by dividing the particulate emissions data by the energy consumption data.
Particulate emissions associated with industrial processes are added to fuel consumption emissions factors by sector.
